claim: The secondary visual cortex (V2) in primates contains a repeating pale-thin-pale-thick stripe pattern of cytochrome oxidase (CO) activity.
source: In primates, visual information sent from the primary visual cortex (V1) to the secondary visual cortex (V2) is segregated into distinct modules known as thin, thick, and pale stripes (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987).

claim: V2 stripes form a columnar system in which functional properties extend roughly through cortical depth.
source: These stripes form a columnar system in the sense that their functional properties extend roughly through cortical depth (Tootell and Hamilton, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tootell and Hamilton, 1989.

claim: Thin stripes are sensitive to color content and project to functional area V4.
source: For example, thin stripes are sensitive to color content and project to functional area V4, whereas thick stripes are more sensitive to binocular disparity and project to area MT (V5) (Shipp and Zeki, 1985; Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Ts'o et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Shipp and Zeki, 1985; Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Ts'o et al., 2001).

claim: Thick stripes are more sensitive to binocular disparity and project to area MT (V5).
source: For example, thin stripes are sensitive to color content and project to functional area V4, whereas thick stripes are more sensitive to binocular disparity and project to area MT (V5) (Shipp and Zeki, 1985; Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Ts'o et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Shipp and Zeki, 1985; Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Ts'o et al., 2001).

claim: V2 stripes were first found in squirrel monkeys and macaques using cytochrome oxidase (CO) staining as dark and pale patches organized in repeating pale-thin-pale-thick cycles.
source: Using cytochrome oxidase (CO) staining, these stripes were found first in squirrel monkeys and macaques as dark and pale patches organized in repeating pale-thin-pale-thick cycles, running through V2 and oriented approximately perpendicular to the V1/V2 border (Livingstone and Hubel, 1982; Tootell et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Livingstone and Hubel, 1982 and Tootell et al., 1983.

claim: In macaques, stripes of the same type have a center-to-center distance of around 4.0 mm and a width ranging from 0.7 to 1.3 mm.
source: In macaques, stripes of the same type have a center-to-center distance of around 4.0 mm and a width ranging from 0.7 to 1.3 mm (Shipp and Zeki, 1985; Tootell and Hamilton, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shipp and Zeki, 1985 and Tootell and Hamilton, 1989.

claim: In humans, stripe widths are approximately doubled in size compared to macaques.
source: In humans, these widths are approximately doubled in size (Hockfield et al., 1990; Tootell and Taylor, 1995; Adams et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hockfield et al., 1990; Tootell and Taylor, 1995; Adams et al., 2007.

claim: Histological studies showed a stripe pattern in V2 of post-mortem brain specimens when myelin staining techniques were used.
source: Histological studies also showed a stripe pattern in V2 of post-mortem brain specimens when techniques for the staining of myelin were used (Tootell et al., 1983; Krubitzer and Kaas, 1989; Horton and Hocking, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tootell et al., 1983; Krubitzer and Kaas, 1989; Horton and Hocking, 1997.

claim: Histological studies gave an inconsistent picture of the correspondence between stripes defined by CO activity and myelin density.
source: However, these studies gave an inconsistent picture of the correspondence between stripes defined by CO activity and myelin density.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of the cited histological studies.

claim: Luxol fast blue staining indicated stronger myelination in thin/thick stripes.
source: Staining with Luxol fast blue indicated stronger myelination in thin/thick (Tootell et al., 1983) stripes, while Gallyas silver staining showed pale (Krubitzer and Kaas, 1989) stripes being more myelinated.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tootell et al., 1983.

claim: Gallyas silver staining showed pale stripes being more myelinated.
source: Staining with Luxol fast blue indicated stronger myelination in thin/thick (Tootell et al., 1983) stripes, while Gallyas silver staining showed pale (Krubitzer and Kaas, 1989) stripes being more myelinated.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krubitzer and Kaas, 1989.

claim: The discrepancy between myelin staining methods was replicated in another study comparing several methods.
source: This discrepancy between myelin staining methods was replicated in another study in which several methods were compared to each other (Horton and Hocking, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Horton and Hocking, 1997.

claim: Standard histochemical methods are highly sensitive to the condition of the brain specimen, variations in fixation and staining procedures, and exposure time.
source: In addition to inconsistencies across staining methods, all standard histochemical methods are highly sensitive to the condition of the brain specimen (e.g. post-mortem delay time), variations in fixation and staining procedures, and exposure time (Savaskan et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Savaskan et al., 2009.

claim: Quantitative MRI (qMRI) aims to isolate one source of image contrast and represent it as a single quantitative parameter map.
source: Quantitative MRI (qMRI) is a collective term of techniques that aims to isolate one source of image contrast and represent it as a single quantitative parameter map, for example, maps of longitudinal relaxation rate (R1), effective transverse relaxation rate (R2*), proton density (PD), or magnetic susceptibility.
evidence: The claim is a definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: qMRI parameter maps are created by combining multiple 'weighted' MR images in a model-based fashion yielding reproducible and standardized measures in physical units.
source: Parameter maps are created by combining multiple 'weighted' MR images in a model-based fashion yielding reproducible and standardized measures in physical units, which are less dependent on the acquisition (Edwards et al., 2018; Trampel et al., 2019; Weiskopf et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 2018; Trampel et al., 2019; Weiskopf et al., 2021.

claim: qMRI provides a closer relationship to specific microstructural components, for example, myelin and iron.
source: Furthermore, by separating different sources of image contrast, qMRI provides a closer relationship to specific microstructural components, for example, myelin and iron (Edwards et al., 2018; Weiskopf et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 2018 and Weiskopf et al., 2021.

claim: Single qMRI parameter maps do not have the specificity to directly infer the abundance of single microstructural tissue components.
source: In this regard, it should be kept in mind that single qMRI parameter maps do not have the specificity to directly infer the abundance of single microstructural tissue components by being sensitive to multiple tissue components to a varying extent and therefore can only serve as a surrogate, for example, in the study of cortical myelination (Lazari and Lipp, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lazari and Lipp, 2021.

claim: Cortical R1 is largely affected by myelin content.
source: Nevertheless, concerning R1, it is known that cortical R1 is largely affected by myelin content (Stüber et al., 2014; Leuze et al., 2017) and, hence, was often used as surrogate to study the macroscopic distribution of cortical myelination (Sigalovsky et al., 2006; Dick et al., 2012; Sereno et al., 2013; Lutti et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stüber et al., 2014 and Leuze et al., 2017.

claim: R1 was often used as a surrogate to study the macroscopic distribution of cortical myelination.
source: Nevertheless, concerning R1, it is known that cortical R1 is largely affected by myelin content (Stüber et al., 2014; Leuze et al., 2017) and, hence, was often used as surrogate to study the macroscopic distribution of cortical myelination (Sigalovsky et al., 2006; Dick et al., 2012; Sereno et al., 2013; Lutti et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sigalovsky et al., 2006; Dick et al., 2012; Sereno et al., 2013; Lutti et al., 2014.

claim: Recent developments in ultra-high field MRI enabled the functional localization of thin and thick stripes using high-resolution fMRI.
source: Functional MRI (fMRI) allows in vivo localization of functional architecture. Recent developments in ultra-high field MRI enabled the functional localization of thin and thick stripes using high-resolution fMRI (Nasr et al., 2016; Dumoulin et al., 2017; Navarro et al., 2021) by, for example, exploiting their different sensitivity to color (Tootell et al., 1983; Tootell et al., 2004) and binocular disparity (Peterhans and von der Heydt, 1993; Chen et al., 2008), respectively (Nasr et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nasr et al., 2016; Dumoulin et al., 2017; Navarro et al., 2021.

claim: The study found lower R1 values in color-selective thin and disparity-selective thick stripes compared to locations containing pale stripe contributions.
source: We robustly show lower R1 values in color-selective thin and disparity-selective thick stripes in comparison to locations containing pale stripe contributions, which points toward higher myelin density in pale stripes.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Lower R1 values in thin and thick stripes point toward higher myelin density in pale stripes.
source: We robustly show lower R1 values in color-selective thin and disparity-selective thick stripes in comparison to locations containing pale stripe contributions, which points toward higher myelin density in pale stripes.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the R1 data based on the known relationship between R1 and myelin content.

claim: No consistent differences in R2* were found between stripe types.
source: No consistent differences were found for effective transverse relaxation rates (R2*).
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: The study demonstrates the feasibility to investigate structure-function relationships in living humans within one cortical area at the level of columnar systems using qMRI.
source: The study demonstrates the feasibility to investigate structure-function relationships in living humans within one cortical area at the level of columnar systems using qMRI.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Four participants were scanned in the study.
source: Participants (n = 4) were invited for multiple fMRI and qMRI sessions at 7 T (see Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section.

claim: High-resolution fMRI was measured at 0.8 mm isotropic resolution.
source: On different days, we measured high-resolution (0.8 mm isotropic) fMRI responses to stimuli varying in color and binocular disparity content, respectively, to locate color-selective thin stripes (color stripes) and disparity-selective thick stripes (disparity stripes) in V2 (Nasr et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section.

claim: The multi-parameter mapping (MPM) protocol was used to acquire high-resolution anatomical images with 0.5 mm isotropic resolution.
source: In a separate session, we used the multi-parameter mapping (MPM) protocol (Vaculčiaková et al., 2022) to acquire high-resolution anatomical images with 0.5 mm isotropic resolution from which quantitative parameter maps (R1, R2*, PD) were derived.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section.

claim: Color-selective stripes are largely confined to CO thin stripes.
source: It should be noted that color-selective stripes are known to be largely confined to CO thin stripes (Xiao et al., 2003; Tootell et al., 2004), whereas selectivity for binocular disparity is found in all stripe types but most frequently in CO thick stripes (Peterhans and von der Heydt, 1993; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xiao et al., 2003 and Tootell et al., 2004.

claim: Selectivity for binocular disparity is found in all stripe types but most frequently in CO thick stripes.
source: It should be noted that color-selective stripes are known to be largely confined to CO thin stripes (Xiao et al., 2003; Tootell et al., 2004), whereas selectivity for binocular disparity is found in all stripe types but most frequently in CO thick stripes (Peterhans and von der Heydt, 1993; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Peterhans and von der Heydt, 1993 and Chen et al., 2008.

claim: No activation was found for binocular disparity in V1.
source: In V1, no activation was found for binocular disparity in Figure 2b which is consistent with findings by Tsao et al., 2003; Nasr et al., 2016, while large V1 activation was found for color contrast in Figure 2a as also shown by Nasr et al., 2016.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b and citations to Tsao et al., 2003 and Nasr et al., 2016.

claim: Large V1 activation was found for color contrast.
source: In V1, no activation was found for binocular disparity in Figure 2b which is consistent with findings by Tsao et al., 2003; Nasr et al., 2016, while large V1 activation was found for color contrast in Figure 2a as also shown by Nasr et al., 2016.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2a and a citation to Nasr et al., 2016.

claim: Activation maps were consistent between sessions of color and disparity stripe measurements.
source: Each stripe type was localized in two independent scanning sessions and activation maps were consistent between sessions of color and disparity stripe measurements, respectively. This is illustrated in Figure 3, which shows statistically significant correlations of activation maps between sessions for one representative participant.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: R1 maps show higher values in primary motor and primary sensory cortical areas, congruent with higher myelin density in these areas.
source: Figure 4a–b shows an R1 map sampled at mid-cortical depth for one representative participant. Primary motor and primary sensory cortical areas have higher R1 values, congruent with higher myelin density in these areas (Flechsig, 1920; Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Sereno et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4a-b and citations to Flechsig, 1920; Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Sereno et al., 2013.

claim: All participants showed increased R1 values in V1 compared to other cortical regions.
source: Figure 4c shows systematic R1 variations with highest values in V1 for each participant, which is in line with Fig. 1(b) in Sereno et al., 2013.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4c and a citation to Sereno et al., 2013.

claim: R1, R2*, and MTVF values decrease toward the pial surface in V2.
source: We also checked cortical profiles of mean parameters in V2 by sampling data on surfaces defined at different cortical depths (see Appendix 2). In all participants, we confirmed the expected decrease of R1, R2*, and MTVF = 100% − PD (macromolecular tissue volume fraction [Mezer et al., 2013]) values toward the pial surface since all three parameters are sensitive to myelin (Marques et al., 2017; Carey et al., 2018; Kirilina et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Appendix 2 and citations to Mezer et al., 2013; Marques et al., 2017; Carey et al., 2018; Kirilina et al., 2020.

claim: Statistically significant differences of R1 were found between thin or thick stripes and mean of V2 excluding the other stripe type.
source: Figure 5a–b shows statistically significant differences of R1 between thin or thick stripes and mean of V2 excluding the other stripe type, which points toward higher myelin density in pale stripes.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: The results for R1 values were confirmed using an independent data set using R1 estimates from the MP2RAGE sequence.
source: These results were confirmed by an independent data set using R1 values estimated from the MP2RAGE sequence (Marques et al., 2010), which is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Marques et al., 2010.

claim: R2* is sensitive to paramagnetic iron and diamagnetic myelin.
source: Whereas R1 in the normal cortex is largely influenced by myelination levels, R2* is sensitive to paramagnetic iron and diamagnetic myelin (Stüber et al., 2014; Kirilina et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stüber et al., 2014 and Kirilina et al., 2020.

claim: Vasculature and the orientation of the cortex to the static magnetic field have an influence on R2*.
source: Other factors like vasculature and the orientation of the cortex to the static magnetic field of the MR system have an influence on R2*, which might have obscured the underlying dependency on myelin content (Cohen-Adad et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cohen-Adad et al., 2012.

claim: Higher vessel densities were found in blobs and stripes of squirrel and macaque monkeys.
source: Indeed, higher vessel densities were found in blobs (another CO-rich structure in V1) and stripes of squirrel and macaque monkeys (Zheng et al., 1991; Keller et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zheng et al., 1991 and Keller et al., 2011.

claim: Another study showed no differences in vascular supply between blobs and inter-blobs in V1.
source: However, this was later disputed by another study, which showed no differences in vascular supply between blobs and inter-blobs in V1 (Adams et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Adams et al., 2015.

claim: R1 differences between stripe types are in the range of around 1–2%.
source: Figure 5a–b shows that R1 differences are in the range of around 1–2%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: R1 differences between cortical areas are in the range of a few percent at 7 T.
source: This is smaller but comparable to R1 differences between cortical areas, which are in the range of a few percent at 7 T (Marques et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marques et al., 2017.

claim: The coefficient of variation in R1 maps was 11.3 ± 0.7 (mean ± standard deviation across participants) in V2.
source: The coefficient of variation in R1 maps was 11.3 ± 0.7 (mean ± standard deviation across participants) in V2.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis described in the text.

claim: The color stimulus with red/blue gratings is expected to have a different effect in the central fovea than in parafoveal regions due to the macula lutea and absence of blue cones in the central fovea.
source: First, the color stimulus with red/blue gratings (see Figure 1a) is expected to have a different effect in the central fovea than in parafoveal regions due to the macula lutea (yellow pigmented spot of the retina) and absence of blue cones in the central fovea, which might have hindered the detection of color stripes there (Nasr and Tootell, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nasr and Tootell, 2018.

claim: Missing activation at the representation of the central fovea for the disparity stimulus could be due to eccentricity dependence of disparity tuning.
source: Second, missing activation at the representation of the central fovea for the disparity stimulus could be due to eccentricity dependence of disparity tuning.
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors.

claim: Tsao et al., 2003 found an overall similar eccentricity-dependent activation pattern for a stimulation with the same maximal disparity (±0.22°).
source: Using conventional fMRI with lower resolution, Tsao et al., 2003, found an overall similar eccentricity-dependent activation pattern for a stimulation with the same maximal disparity (±0.22°).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tsao et al., 2003.

claim: Spatial overlap of activation maps for color-selective thin and disparity-selective thick stripes is expected to some degree and mainly driven by the limiting physiological point spread function of the measured blood oxygenation level-dependent signal in fMRI.
source: It should be kept in mind that spatial overlap is expected to some degree and mainly driven by the limiting physiological point spread function of the measured blood oxygenation level-dependent signal in fMRI (Polimeni et al., 2010; Chaimow et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Polimeni et al., 2010 and Chaimow et al., 2018.

claim: Differential contrasts between two experimental conditions are known to be less affected by unspecific macrovascular contributions and draining veins.
source: We based the ROI definition on activation maps from differential contrasts between two experimental conditions as illustrated in Figure 1a–b, which are known to be less affected by unspecific macrovascular contributions and draining veins.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pistorio et al., 2006 showed in monkey V1 that the edges of blobs are more myelinated rather than blobs or inter-blob regions itself using a modified Gallyas stain.
source: Pistorio et al., 2006, showed in monkey V1 that the edges of blobs are more myelinated rather than blobs or inter-blob regions itself using a modified Gallyas stain.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pistorio et al., 2006.

claim: An optical tracking system was used to prospectively correct head movements during anatomical scans.
source: Measurements with high resolution are vulnerable to head movements during image acquisition, especially for the long anatomical scans. Therefore, we used an optical tracking system to prospectively correct head movements during anatomical scans (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The equi-volume model was used to sample at mid-cortical depth.
source: We used the equi-volume model to sample at mid-cortical depth. This model has been shown to be less affected by curvature biases than other models (e.g. equi-distant sampling) (Waehnert et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to Waehnert et al., 2014.

claim: The equi-volume model has been shown to be less affected by curvature biases than other models.
source: We used the equi-volume model to sample at mid-cortical depth. This model has been shown to be less affected by curvature biases than other models (e.g. equi-distant sampling) (Waehnert et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Waehnert et al., 2014.

claim: Remaining curvature contributions were regressed out as in other studies.
source: Remaining curvature contributions were regressed out as in other studies (Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Sereno et al., 2013; Dumoulin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Sereno et al., 2013; Dumoulin et al., 2017.

claim: The findings point toward higher myelination of pale stripes which exhibit lower oxidative metabolic activity according to staining with CO.
source: Our findings point toward higher myelination of pale stripes which exhibit lower oxidative metabolic activity according to staining with CO.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: V2 receives most of its input from V1 and the pulvinar.
source: V2 receives most of its input from V1 and the pulvinar (Tootell et al., 1983; Sincich and Horton, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tootell et al., 1983 and Sincich and Horton, 2005.

claim: Pulvinar projections only terminate in layers 3 and 5.
source: Pulvinar projections, however, only terminate in layers 3 and 5, whereas the alternating myelin pattern is most obvious in layer 4, which receives input almost exclusively from V1 (Tootell et al., 1983; Sincich and Horton, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tootell et al., 1983 and Sincich and Horton, 2005.

claim: The alternating myelin pattern is most obvious in layer 4, which receives input almost exclusively from V1.
source: Pulvinar projections, however, only terminate in layers 3 and 5, whereas the alternating myelin pattern is most obvious in layer 4, which receives input almost exclusively from V1 (Tootell et al., 1983; Sincich and Horton, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tootell et al., 1983 and Sincich and Horton, 2005.

claim: Sincich and Horton, 2002 showed that [3H]proline injections into V1 preferentially targeted V2 pale stripes.
source: An anterograde tracer study in macaques by Sincich and Horton, 2002, showed that [3H]proline injections into V1 preferentially targeted V2 pale stripes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sincich and Horton, 2002.

claim: The results of Sincich and Horton, 2002 might correspond to higher axonal density of V1 to V2 projections in layer 4 of pale stripes.
source: Although we cannot exclude that systematic differences in terminal axonal arborization between stripe types could explain this observation, we speculate that the results of that study correspond to higher axonal density of V1 to V2 projections in layer 4 of pale stripes.
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors.

claim: Higher axonal density of V1 to V2 projections in layer 4 of pale stripes would lead to higher myelination in pale stripes.
source: This would lead to higher myelination in pale stripes, which is in line with our measurements.
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors based on inference.

claim: The study shows the feasibility to use high-resolution quantitative R1 values to study cortical myelination.
source: By comparing myelin-sensitive longitudinal relaxation rates (R1) between stripe types in V2 defined by high-resolution fMRI, we found significant quantitative evidence for myelination differences in living humans at the level of columnar systems. This shows the feasibility to use high-resolution quantitative R1 values to study cortical myelination, which is known to be less biased by technical artifacts and are thus better comparable among participants and scanner sites.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Quantitative R1 values are known to be less biased by technical artifacts and are thus better comparable among participants and scanner sites.
source: This shows the feasibility to use high-resolution quantitative R1 values to study cortical myelination, which is known to be less biased by technical artifacts and are thus better comparable among participants and scanner sites.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The myelination of cortical areas and structures affects their functional properties, that is, the propagation of action potentials.
source: Moreover, it is well known that the myelination of cortical areas and structures affects their functional properties, that is, the propagation of action potentials (Sanders and Whitteridge, 1946), and correlates with postnatal development (Glasser and Van Essen, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sanders and Whitteridge, 1946 and Glasser and Van Essen, 2011.

claim: Myelination correlates with postnatal development.
source: Moreover, it is well known that the myelination of cortical areas and structures affects their functional properties, that is, the propagation of action potentials (Sanders and Whitteridge, 1946), and correlates with postnatal development (Glasser and Van Essen, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Glasser and Van Essen, 2011.

claim: Four healthy participants (1 female, age = 27.50 ± 4.39, mean ± standard deviation) gave written informed consent to participate in this study.
source: Four healthy participants (1 female, age = 27.50 ± 4.39, mean ± standard deviation) gave written informed consent to participate in this study.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committee of the University of Leipzig (reference number: 273–14).
source: The study was approved by the local ethics committee of the University of Leipzig (reference number: 273–14).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity, normal color vision, and normal stereoscopic vision.
source: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity, normal color vision (based on Ishihara and Farnsworth D15 tests), and normal stereoscopic vision (based on Lang I test).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Each participant was scanned multiple times on different days in an ultra-high field MR scanner (7 T).
source: Each participant was scanned multiple times on different days in an ultra-high field MR scanner (7 T).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Color-selective thin stripes were mapped in two sessions.
source: Color-selective thin stripes (two sessions) and disparity-selective thick stripes (two sessions) were mapped in subsequent scanning sessions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Disparity-selective thick stripes were mapped in two sessions.
source: Color-selective thin stripes (two sessions) and disparity-selective thick stripes (two sessions) were mapped in subsequent scanning sessions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Stimuli for color-selective thin stripe mapping consisted of isoluminant sinusoidal color-varying (red/blue) or luminance-varying (black/white) gratings.
source: Stimuli consisted of isoluminant sinusoidal color-varying (red/blue) or luminance-varying (black/white) gratings as illustrated in Figure 1a.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: A low spatial frequency (0.4 cpd) was used to mitigate linear chromatic aberration at color borders and exploit the relatively higher selectivity to color relative to luminance at this spatial scale.
source: A low spatial frequency (0.4 cpd) was used to mitigate linear chromatic aberration at color borders and exploit the relatively higher selectivity to color relative to luminance at this spatial scale (Tootell and Nasr, 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation to Tootell and Nasr, 2017.

claim: The appropriateness to use red and blue colors to stimulate color-selective thin stripes has already been demonstrated for macaques and humans.
source: We point out that the appropriateness to use red and blue colors to stimulate color-selective thin stripes has already been demonstrated for macaques (Tootell et al., 2004; Li et al., 2019) and humans (Nasr et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tootell et al., 2004; Li et al., 2019; Nasr et al., 2016.

claim: Isoluminance points between colors are known to change with eccentricity.
source: Furthermore, isoluminance points between colors are known to change with eccentricity (Livingstone and Hubel, 1987; Bilodeau and Faubert, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Livingstone and Hubel, 1987 and Bilodeau and Faubert, 1997.

claim: Flicker photometry was used to get isoluminance ratios between stimuli for each participant.
source: We used a flicker photometry (Ives, 1907; Bone and Landrum, 2004) paradigm to get isoluminance ratios between stimuli for each participant.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citations to Ives, 1907 and Bone and Landrum, 2004.

claim: Stimuli for disparity-selective thick stripe mapping consisted of two overlaid random dot stereograms (RDSs) made of red and green dots on a black background.
source: Stimuli consisted of two overlaid random dot stereograms (RDSs) (Blakemore and Julesz, 1971) made of red and green dots on a black background (dot size: 0.1°, dot density: ∼17%), respectively.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation to Blakemore and Julesz, 1971.

claim: Maximal disparity was set to ±0.22°.
source: Maximal disparity was set to ±0.22° (Tsao et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation to Tsao et al., 2003.

claim: All experiments were performed on a 7 T whole-body MR scanner.
source: All experiments were performed on a 7 T whole-body MR scanner (MAGNETOM 7 T, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with SC72 body gradients (maximum gradient strength: 70 mT/m; maximum slew rate: 200 mT/m/s).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A single-channel transmit/32-channel receive head coil was used for RF signal transmission and reception.
source: For radio frequency (RF) signal transmission and reception, a single-channel transmit/32-channel receive head coil (Nova Medical, Wilmington, DE, USA) was used.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Functional data was acquired with a 2D single-shot gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence.
source: Functional data was acquired with a 2D single-shot gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence (Feinberg et al., 2010; Moeller et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citations to Feinberg et al., 2010 and Moeller et al., 2010.

claim: MR relaxation parameters (R1, R2*, PD) were measured with a multi-echo variable flip angle protocol for multi-parameter mapping (MPM).
source: MR relaxation parameters (R1, R2*, PD) were measured with a multi-echo variable flip angle protocol for multi-parameter mapping (MPM) (Vaculčiaková et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation to Vaculčiaková et al., 2022.

claim: Head movements during the MPM scan were corrected prospectively using an optical tracking system.
source: Head movements during the scan were corrected prospectively using an optical tracking system (Kineticor, USA).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A whole-brain anatomy was acquired using a 3D T1-weighted MP2RAGE sequence.
source: For cortex segmentation and image registration, a whole-brain anatomy was acquired using a 3D T1-weighted MP2RAGE sequence (Marques et al., 2010) with the following parameters: voxel size = 0.7 mm isotropic, TR = 5000 ms, TE = 2.45 ms, inversion times (TI1/TI2) = 900 ms/2750 ms with FA = 5°/3° for T1w and PDw images, respectively, FOV = 224 × 224 × 168 mm3 (read × phase × partition), rBW = 250 Hz/px, partial Fourier = 6/8, and GRAPPA = 2 (primary phase-encoding direction; outer loop).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation to Marques et al., 2010.

claim: Quantitative parameter maps (R1, R2*, PD) were computed using the hMRI toolbox.
source: Quantitative parameter maps (R1, R2*, PD) were computed using the hMRI toolbox (Tabelow et al., 2019) (0.2.2, http://hmri.info) implemented in SPM12 (v7487).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation to Tabelow et al., 2019.

claim: Cortex segmentation was based on the MP2RAGE UNI image.
source: Cortex segmentation was based on the MP2RAGE UNI image.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The recon-all pipeline in FreeSurfer was used for cortex segmentation.
source: The resulting image was input to the recon-all pipeline in FreeSurfer (Dale et al., 1999; Fischl et al., 1999) (6.0.0, http://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/) with the hires flag to segment at the original voxel resolution (Zaretskaya et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citations to Dale et al., 1999; Fischl et al., 1999; Zaretskaya et al., 2018.

claim: A surface mesh at mid-cortical depth was computed using the equi-volume model.
source: A surface mesh at mid-cortical depth was computed using the equi-volume model (Waehnert et al., 2014; Wagstyl et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citations to Waehnert et al., 2014 and Wagstyl et al., 2018.

claim: The BrainSMASH package was used to preserve the spatial autocorrelation in spatially shuffled maps.
source: We paid attention to preserve the spatial autocorrelation in spatially shuffled maps using the BrainSMASH package (Burt et al., 2020) (0.10.0) to consider the non-independence of data from neighboring locations.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation to Burt et al., 2020.
